 CARPHA strengthens dengue preparedness in Trinidad, Bahamas
 Last updated: 19 Nov 2026 | 1:58 PM | AST 
 Press Release 
 Published: 19 Nov 2026 | 1:58 PM | AST 
 Disclosure: This website may contains affiliate links. 
 The Caribbean Public Health Agency (CARPHA) has strengthened national capacity to anticipate and respond to dengue threats through two country-level training workshops held in Trinidad and Tobago on 5–6 November 2026, and The Bahamas on 10–11 November 2026.
 Titled “Dengue Ready: Country Training on Climate-Informed Dengue Risk Prediction Platforms”, the workshops brought together 31 participants in Trinidad and Tobago and 25 participants in The Bahamas, including professionals working in public health, vector control and meteorology. The training focused on using climate and disease surveillance data to forecast dengue risks and support more timely and informed public health interventions.
 Delivered by CARPHA, in collaboration with the Global Council for Science and the Environment and the Barcelona Supercomputing Center, the training formed part of CARPHA’s wider climate and health initiatives.
 Both workshops were supported through the CARPHA’s Pandemic Fund project, with CARPHA serving as the Executing Agency and the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) as the Implementing Entity.
 Highlighting the importance of collaboration in addressing climate-sensitive health threats, CARPHA Executive Director, Dr. Lisa Indar, emphasised the value of strengthening national and regional capacity. “CARPHA recognises that Dengue preparedness is not solely a health-sector responsibility. We are pleased to facilitate this training which brings together public health, meteorological and vector control professionals around country-specific tools. Through this approach, we are strengthening the partnerships and capabilities that countries need to protect their communities in a changing climate,” Dr. Indar emphasised.
 The country-level training marked another milestone in a programme of work that began in June 2025, followed by the completion of a feasibility study in December 2025. Preparatory activities included engagement with national stakeholders, arrangements for accessing relevant data, collection of epidemiological and meteorological datasets, and the development of country-specific dengue risk prediction platforms.
 The training also built on earlier climate-informed dengue modelling and capacity-building activities in Barbados, Saint Lucia and Grenada, as well as the regional Climate and Health Workshop for Vector-borne Disease Preparedness held in Barbados on 8–9 September 2026. The workshops in Trinidad and Tobago and The Bahamas advanced these regional efforts through practical training on the use of the platforms and discussions on their implementation at the national level.
 Underscoring the need for a more proactive approach to dengue preparedness, Dr. Horace Cox, Director of CARPHA’s Surveillance, Disease Prevention and Control Division, highlighted the importance of using scientific evidence to inform public health decisions. “The reality is clear: we can no longer rely solely on reacting to outbreaks after they occur. We must increasingly anticipate risk, act earlier, and use the best available science to guide public health decision-making,” he emphasised.
 In Trinidad and Tobago, participants included representatives from the Ministry of Health, the Ministry of Rural Development and Local Government, and the Trinidad and Tobago Meteorological Service. In The Bahamas, participants represented the Ministry of Health and Wellness, the Ministry of the Environment and Natural Resources through its Department of Environmental Health Services, and The Bahamas Department of Meteorology.
 During these two-day workshops, participants explored the development and functionality of the dengue risk prediction platforms and examined how forecasting models generate alerts and risk levels. Guided exercises provided practical experience in navigating the platforms, understanding data requirements, and identifying responsibilities for data submission and updates.
 Participants also practised interpreting platform outputs and visualisations, considered how the information could inform dengue surveillance and response measures, and provided feedback on additional features and data needs. Practical sessions introduced the Global Health Resilience and Data for Health R packages for climate and health analysis, while monitoring and evaluation discussions addressed how the platforms’ use and performance could be assessed over time.
 An important component of the training was the proposed integration of climate-informed dengue forecasting with CARPHA’s Regional Integrated Early Warning and Surveillance System (RIEWSS). CARPHA outlined the technical requirements and potential pathway for future integration, which would support efforts to strengthen early warning and surveillance capabilities across the Region.
 Speaking at the workshop in The Bahamas, Dr. Parasram, Head of Vector-Borne Diseases at CARPHA, highlighted the importance of translating early warning information into effective public health interventions. “The true measure of success will be the consistent use of this system to inform earlier, coordinated action: targeted vector control, purposeful community communication and health-service readiness,” he stressed.
 Feedback gathered during the workshops will inform further refinement of the country-specific platforms and technical planning for their future integration with RIEWSS. The training represents another step towards supporting countries in making greater use of climate-informed information to strengthen dengue preparedness, surveillance and public health response.
